question: What is the file extension of a Java source code file, the kind you type and save yourself?
correct: .java
incorrect: .class
.jar
.javac
feedback: You write source code in a .java file. A .class file holds compiled code rather than source, a .jar is a bundle of compiled files packed together for sharing, and javac is the name of a tool, not a file ending.

question: Typing {{1}} Hello.java in a terminal compiles the source into a bytecode file named Hello.{{2}}; typing {{3}} Hello then starts the program.
feedback: javac is the compiler (the c is for compiler): it translates Hello.java into bytecode and saves it as Hello.class. java is the launcher: it starts the Java Virtual Machine and hands it that bytecode. Note that the launcher is given the class name, Hello, with no extension.

question: Arrange the life of a classic Java program from the first step to the last.
items: You type the source code and save it as a .java file
You run the compiler on that file
The compiler writes out a file of bytecode
The launcher starts the JVM, which loads the bytecode
The statements inside main run one after another
feedback: Source comes first, because the compiler needs something to read. The compiler has to finish before there is any bytecode, the JVM (Java Virtual Machine) can only load bytecode that exists, and main cannot begin until the JVM has loaded it. Bytecode is the same on every computer; the JVM is the part that differs from machine to machine.

question:
On JDK 25, a folder holds the file Hello.java and nothing else. You type:
java Hello.java
What happens?
correct: The source is compiled in memory and then run, and no .class file is left behind
incorrect: The launcher reports an error, since it accepts class names and not source files
The source is compiled to Hello.class on disk, and that file is then run as usual
The source is run line by line as written, so no compilation takes place at all
feedback: Give the java launcher a file name ending in .java and it compiles that file in memory, then runs it. That is handy for one-file programs. Compilation is not skipped, only hidden, so compiler errors still appear. Nothing is written to disk, which is why the folder still holds only Hello.java afterwards. For a project with many files you still compile first.

question: Java 25 accepts several forms of the main method, including a bare  void main() . Which of these is the classic form, the one the java launcher accepts in every version of Java?
correct: public static void main(String[] args)
incorrect: public static void Main(String[] args)
public static int main(String[] args)
public static void main(String args)
feedback: The classic form is public static void main(String[] args), and it is the one you will meet in nearly all existing code. Each wrong option changes one piece. Java is case-sensitive, so Main is a different name. main hands nothing back, so its return type is void and not int. And the parameter is an array of Strings, which needs the [] brackets. With any of those three, the launcher reports that it cannot find a main method.

question: Which statements about a classic Java program (a class that contains a main method) are true?
correct: If the class is declared public, the file name has to match the class name
When the program starts, the first statement inside main is the first to run
A statement is ended by its semicolon, and a line break alone does not end it
incorrect: An import line is needed before the program is able to use System.out
Taking out the indentation would stop the program from compiling
The class has to be named Main for the launcher to be able to find it
feedback: A public class named Hello has to live in Hello.java, or the compiler complains. Execution starts at the top of main and works downward. Java finds the end of a statement by its semicolon, so line breaks and indentation are for human readers: unlike Python, Java ignores them. System lives in the java.lang package, which every Java file can use with no import. The class can have any legal name; it is the method that is called main.

question: What does  System.out.println("Hi")  do that  System.out.print("Hi")  does not?
correct: Ends the line after the text, so later output starts below it
incorrect: Starts a fresh line before the text, so the text sits by itself
Accepts numbers as well as text, where print accepts text alone
Adds a space after the text, so later output is kept separate
feedback: The ln stands for line: println prints the text and then ends the line. The line break comes after the text, not before it, so the first thing a program prints is not pushed down a line. print does everything println does except that: it takes numbers and variables just as happily, and neither of them adds any spaces.

question: What exactly does this print? (Type the output, keeping any line breaks.)
correct:
Golem!
ok
feedback: print leaves the cursor where it is, so Go, lem and ! all land on one line with nothing between them: neither method adds spaces. The first println ends that line after the !, so ok starts on the next one.

question: Each of these String literals is handed to System.out.println. Match each literal to what appears on the screen.

pairs.definition: hi and yo, on two separate lines
hi and yo on one line, with a wide tab gap between
hi and yo on one line, with one backslash between
hi and yo on one line, with one quote mark between

feedback: Inside a String literal a backslash starts an escape sequence: a two-character code for something you cannot type directly. \n is a newline and \t is a tab. Because the backslash and the double quote already have jobs inside a literal, you write \\ to get one real backslash and \" to get one real quote mark.

question: Write the Java statement that declares an int variable named score and gives it the value 0.
correct: int score = 0;
var score = 0;
feedback: The type comes first, then the name, then = and the starting value, then a semicolon: int score = 0; Writing var score = 0; works as well. With var the compiler works out the type from the value on the right, and a plain 0 is an int.

question: Which of these would Java accept as the name of a variable?
correct: _price
myVar2
incorrect: 2cups
coffee-price
class
total cost
feedback: A name may use letters, digits, underscores and dollar signs, and may not begin with a digit. So _price and myVar2 are legal and 2cups is not. In coffee-price the hyphen is the subtraction operator, so Java reads it as coffee minus price. A space ends a name, so total cost is two names. And class is a reserved word: Java keeps it for its own use.

question: Two of these lines contain comments. What does the program print?
feedback: Everything from // to the end of that line is a comment, which the compiler ignores. The whole of line 2 is a comment, so the + 10 never happens. On line 3 only the note after the semicolon is a comment, so x = x * 2 still runs, and 4 doubled is printed.

correct: The compiler rejects them, since total has not been given a value
incorrect: They print 0, since an int variable starts out holding zero
They print whatever number was left behind in that memory
They compile, and then crash when the println line is reached
feedback: javac checks that every local variable is given a value before it is read, and refuses to compile if it cannot be sure: the message is 'variable total might not have been initialized'. Java will not quietly supply a zero for a local variable, and it will not let you see leftover memory the way C can. Because the compiler stops it, the program never gets far enough to crash.

question: Which of these lines compile?
correct: boolean isOpen = true;
boolean isDecaf = false;
incorrect: boolean isOpen = 1;
boolean isOpen = "true";
boolean isOpen = True;
feedback: A boolean holds true or false, written in lower case, and nothing else. Java will not treat 1 as true. "true" in double quotes is a String, which is text, not a boolean. And Java is case-sensitive, unlike Python's True: Java takes True for the name of a variable it has never heard of and reports 'cannot find symbol'.

question: Which claims about Java's primitive types are correct?
correct: An int occupies 32 bits, and its largest value is a little over 2 billion
A long can hold whole numbers that are too large to fit into an int
A double can hold a fraction such as 2.5, which an int is unable to hold
incorrect: Adding 1 to the largest possible int stops the program with an error
A double holds each decimal exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 prints as 0.3
feedback: An int is a 32-bit whole number running from about -2.1 billion to +2.1 billion; a long has 64 bits and reaches far further. Going past the top of an int raises no error: the value silently wraps round to the most negative int, which is a nasty bug to find. A double holds fractions, but in binary, so many decimals are stored as very close approximations: 0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004.

question: Write the Java statement that declares a String variable named s holding the two-letter text Hi.
correct: String s = "Hi";
var s = "Hi";
feedback: String s = "Hi"; The type is spelled String with a capital S (lower-case string is not a Java type), a single = assigns, and text goes in double quotes. Single quotes are for exactly one character, so 'Hi' will not compile. var s = "Hi"; is also fine: the compiler sees the text and makes s a String.

question: Which statements about Java Strings are true?
correct: String is spelled with a capital S, as it is a class and not a primitive
Joining a String and an int with + gives a result that is a String
incorrect: "A" and 'A' are two ways of writing one and the same value
A String literal may be wrapped in single or in double quotes
Joining two Strings with + puts a single space between them
feedback: String is a class, which is why it has a capital letter like other class names; int, double, boolean and char are the lower-case primitives. Double quotes make a String and single quotes make a char, which is a different type holding exactly one character, so "A" and 'A' are not interchangeable. The + operator joins text exactly as it stands: "a" + "b" is "ab", and if you want a space you put it inside the quotes. When one side of + is a String, the other side is turned into text and the result is a String.

question: NPC: Seventeen coins, five adventurers
intro: Ada tips a pouch of 17 coins onto the workbench. “Five adventurers, seventeen coins. Java shares them out exactly the way a fair paymaster would — and that surprises people.”

steps.say: Java has two operators for sharing things out. Here they are, both working on whole numbers — ints. Deal the coins: everyone gets 3, which uses up 15. When both sides of / are ints, Java does integer division: it keeps the whole number and throws the fraction away.

beats.say: Java has two operators for sharing things out. Here they are, both working on whole numbers — ints.
Deal the coins round the table: everyone gets 3, and that uses up 15 of them.
That is what / does when both sides are ints. It is called integer division: Java keeps the whole number and throws the fraction away.

check.prompt: So what does 17 / 5 give when both numbers are ints?
check.why: Integer division keeps only the whole part. It does not round, either: 3.4 becomes 3, and 3.9 would become 3 as well.

steps.say: Two coins are still lying in the pouch. That is what % gives you: the remainder, whatever is left over once the sharing is done. So left holds 2.

check.prompt: Try one. 14 coins among 4 adventurers: what are 14 / 4 and 14 % 4?
check.why: 4 fits into 14 three whole times, using 12 coins, so / gives 3. The 2 coins left over are what % gives.

steps.say: The pattern: / says how many whole times it fits, % says what is left over. If you want the fraction kept, make one side a double — 17 / 5.0 — and Java gives 3.4.

beats.say: The pattern: with ints, / says how many whole times it fits, and % says what is left over.
And if you do want the fraction? Make either side a double — write 17 / 5.0 — and Java keeps it: 3.4.

outro: “The next monsters will throw fresh numbers at you. Deal the coins in your head.”

question:
Both numbers are ints. What is the value of this Java expression?
{{a}} / {{b}}
feedback_template: With an int on both sides, / is integer division: {{b}} fits into {{a}} exactly {{expected}} whole times, and any fraction left over is thrown away. It is not rounded, so even a fraction of .9 disappears.

question:
Both numbers are ints. What is the value of this Java expression?
{{a}} % {{b}}
feedback_template: % gives the remainder. Take as many whole {{b}}s out of {{a}} as will fit (possibly none at all) and {{expected}} is what is left. When the left number is the smaller one, nothing can be taken out, so the remainder is the left number itself.

feedback: Java works out the right-hand side before it looks at where the answer is going. Both 7 and 2 are ints, so 7 / 2 is integer division and the fraction is already gone by the time the result is stored in the double. Storing it in a double only adds the .0 to what is left. To keep the half, make either operand a double, as in 7 / 2.0.

question: Match each Java expression to the type of the value it produces.
feedback: Two ints divided give an int, fraction discarded. Put a double on either side and the whole result becomes a double. Single quotes make a char, which is one character; double quotes make a String, even when the text inside is a digit. A comparison such as > does not produce a number at all: it produces true or false, a boolean.

feedback_template: This is the standard way to split a total into a big unit and a small one. total / 60 is integer division, so it gives the number of whole hours in {{t}} minutes; total % 60 gives the minutes left over once those hours are taken out. Both are ints, so the + adds them, giving {{expected}}.

question: Which of these jobs is the % operator suited to?
correct: Checking whether a whole number is even or odd
Wrapping a counter back round to 0 when it reaches a limit
Testing whether one whole number divides evenly into another
Pulling the last digit off the end of a whole number
incorrect: Working out what percentage one number is of another
Rounding a decimal number to the nearest whole number
feedback: Every real use of % comes from asking what is left over. n % 2 is 0 for even numbers and 1 for odd ones. count % 12 can never reach 12, so it wraps back to 0. If a % b is 0 then b divides a with nothing left. And n % 10 is the last digit: 137 % 10 is 7. Despite the symbol, % has nothing to do with percentages, which need * and /. It does not round anything either.

question:
What is the value of this Java expression?
{{a}} + {{b}} * {{c}} - {{d}}
feedback_template: * ranks above + and -, so {{b}} * {{c}} is worked out first, wherever it sits in the line. After that, + and - have equal rank and are applied left to right: add {{a}}, then take away {{d}}, which gives {{expected}}. Working strictly left to right from the start gives a different, wrong number.

question:
All three numbers are ints. What is the value of this Java expression?
{{a}} + {{b}} / {{c}}
feedback_template: Two rules at once. / ranks above +, so {{b}} / {{c}} is done first; and with two ints that is integer division, so it gives {{k}} and the fraction is dropped. Only then is {{a}} added, giving {{expected}}.

question:
What value is stored in avg?
int avg = ({{a}} + {{b}}) / 2;
feedback_template: Parentheses go first, so the two numbers are added before anything is divided. The sum is odd, and an int divided by an int drops the half, leaving {{expected}}. Without the parentheses only {{b}} would have been divided by 2.

question: Which claims about the order in which Java evaluates arithmetic are correct?
correct: The operators *, / and % are all applied before + and - are
10 - 4 - 3 is 3, since operators of equal rank go left to right
Adding parentheses can change the value an expression produces
incorrect: Addition is done before multiplication when it comes first in the line
% is applied after + and -, as it is not one of the four basic operations
feedback: Java ranks operators the way school arithmetic does: *, / and % share the higher rank, + and - share the lower. Position in the line does not change that, so a multiplication further along is still done before an earlier addition. Within one rank Java goes left to right, which is why 10 - 4 - 3 is 3 and not 9. Parentheses are always worked out first, so they can change the result. % belongs with * and /: 2 + 7 % 3 is 3.

question: NPC: Shorthand that changes a variable
intro: Nia chalks five lines on the wall and draws an empty box beside them, labelled hp. “Shorthand operators. Quick to write, easy to misread. So we do not read them — we trace them.”

steps.say: One box for the variable hp. Line one puts 5 in it. hp += 3 is shorthand for hp = hp + 3: take the old value, add 3, store the result back. The box now says 8.

beats.say: One box for the variable hp. Line one puts 5 in the box.
hp += 3 is shorthand for hp = hp + 3. Take the old value, add 3, store the result back. The box now says 8.

check.prompt: The next line is hp++. What does the box say now?
check.why: ++ adds exactly 1 and stores it back: hp++ does the same job as hp = hp + 1.

steps.say: Last one: hp *= 2 means hp = hp * 2. It is the same pattern every time. -=, *=, /= and %= all mean: do this to the old value, and store the result back in the same variable.

check.prompt: The box says 9. After hp *= 2, what does the last line print?
check.why: *= multiplies: 9 * 2 is 18, and 18 replaces the 9 in the box. 11 would be the answer for += 2.

steps.say: One box, one line at a time, and the newest value wins. These are called compound assignment operators, and none of them does anything you could not write the long way.

outro: “A monster ahead has four lines of its own, with different numbers. Draw the box.”

feedback_template: Trace it one line at a time, always using the newest value. += {{b}} adds {{b}} to the {{a}}; ++ adds 1 more; *= 2 doubles whatever n holds by then; -= {{c}} takes {{c}} away, leaving {{expected}}. Each shorthand line reads the old value, works on it, and stores the result back in n.

question: Dividing by 5 and then multiplying by 5 looks as if it should undo itself. What does this print?
feedback: x /= 5 means x = x / 5, and with ints that is integer division: x becomes 3 and the remainder of 2 is gone for good. Multiplying back gives 15, not the original number, and ++ makes it 16. Once integer division has thrown a fraction away, no later step can recover it.

correct: The compiler rejects line 2, since a final variable cannot be given a new value
incorrect: The program prints 20, since final is a naming hint that is not enforced
The program prints 10, since the assignment on line 2 is quietly skipped
The program compiles, and then crashes when it reaches line 2
feedback: final makes a variable a constant: it can be given a value once and never again. The rule is enforced by the compiler, whose message is 'cannot assign a value to final variable MAX_HP', so the program never starts. It is the word final that does this. The capital letters are only a convention for naming constants, and they have no effect by themselves.

question: Java programmers follow naming conventions so that a name shows what kind of thing it is. Match each name to what it most likely refers to.
feedback: Variables and methods use camelCase: lower case first, then a capital at the start of each later word. Classes do the same but start with a capital, which is why String and System look the way they do. Constants are written in capitals with underscores between the words. Package names are all lower case, with dots between the parts. The compiler enforces none of this, but every Java programmer reads code by it.

question: Which of these declarations compile?
correct: var n = 10;
var name = "Ada";
var price = 4.50;
incorrect: var x;
var count = 1, total = 2;
feedback: var tells the compiler to work out the type from the value on the right-hand side: 10 makes an int, "Ada" a String, 4.50 a double. That is why var x; fails: with no value there is nothing to work the type out from, and the compiler reports 'cannot infer type'. var also insists on one variable per declaration, so the line declaring both count and total is rejected.

correct: Refuses to compile them, since n became an int on line 1
incorrect: Runs them, since a var variable may hold a value of any type
Compiles them, and then crashes when line 2 is reached
Runs them, but n keeps 10 as the types do not match
feedback: var does not mean 'any type'. It means 'compiler, you work out the type', and that happens once, at the declaration: n is an int from line 1 onward, exactly as if int n = 10; had been written. Putting text into an int is a type mismatch, which the compiler catches ('String cannot be converted to int') before the program can run. This is the big difference from Python and JavaScript, where a variable can change type as it goes.

question: NPC: When + stops adding
intro: Nia holds up a shop receipt that reads Total: 23. “Two potions and three scrolls. Five items. The program says twenty-three, and nothing crashed. So let us find out what + really did.”

steps.say: + has two jobs. Between two numbers it adds. If either side is a String it joins instead — that is called concatenation — and the result is a String. Java works through a chain of + from left to right, so first comes "Total: " + 2, which joins to make "Total: 2".

beats.say: Here is the line that printed the receipt.
+ has two jobs. Between two numbers, it adds. But if either side is a String, it joins the two into one longer String. That joining is called concatenation.
Java works through a chain of + from left to right. The first + has a String on its left, so it joins, and we have the String "Total: 2".

check.prompt: Now the second +. It sees "Total: 2" on its left and 3 on its right. What is the result?
check.why: The left side is a String by now, so + joins again. The 2 and the 3 never meet as numbers.

steps.say: Flip it round. Left to right again: 2 + 3 comes first, and both sides are numbers, so this time + adds.

beats.say: Now flip it round.
Left to right again. The first + has a number on both sides, so this time it really adds.

check.why: 2 + 3 is worked out first and gives the number 5. Only then does + meet a String, and it joins 5 to " total".

steps.say: So: numbers that come before the first String get added, and everything after it gets joined on. To get a sum after the text, wrap it in parentheses — "Total: " + (2 + 3) — because parentheses are worked out first.

beats.say: So: numbers that come before the first String are added. Everything after it is joined on, one piece at a time.
Want a real sum after the text? Wrap it in parentheses, because parentheses are worked out first.

outro: “The next monster puts numbers on both sides of the text. Go left to right, one + at a time.”

question: Work through the + signs from left to right. What does this print?
feedback: The first + has a number on each side, so it adds: 3. The next + has the String "a" on its right, so it joins: "3a". From then on the left side is always a String, so the last 1 and 2 are joined on one at a time, not added. The very same pair of numbers gives 3 before the text and 12 after it.

question:
The output of this line happens to be made of digits alone. What number appears on the screen?
System.out.println({{a}} + {{b}} + "" + {{a}} + {{b}});
feedback_template: Left to right: the first + sits between two numbers, so it adds them. Next comes "", an empty String. It adds no characters, but it is still a String, so from there on every + joins. The second {{a}} and {{b}} are written out one after the other as digits, and the screen shows {{expected}}.

question: These five lines come from a program that asks for an age and prints the age next year. (The class line, the main line and the closing braces have been left out.) Arrange them in the order they appear in the file, top to bottom.
feedback: The import goes at the very top of the file, above the class: it tells the compiler where Scanner lives. Inside main, each line needs the one before it. A Scanner wrapped around System.in (the keyboard) has to exist before it can read, age has to be read before it can be used in a sum, and next has to be worked out before it can be printed.

question: A Scanner named in is reading from the keyboard. Calling in.{{1}}() reads the next whole number as an int, in.{{2}}() reads the next decimal number as a double, and in.{{3}}() reads the rest of the current line as a String.
feedback: Scanner has one method for each kind of value, all named next-something in camelCase, and the capital letter matters because Java is case-sensitive. nextInt and nextDouble turn what was typed into a number of that type, ready for arithmetic. nextLine hands back the text exactly as typed, as a String.

question: NPC: Three moments a program can go wrong
intro: Ada pins a two-line program to the board. “A program can fail at three different moments. Know which moment you are looking at, and you know where to hunt.”

steps.say: Look at the end of line one: no semicolon. The compiler reads the whole program before any of it runs, and it refuses this. That is a compile-time error: caught before the program starts.

beats.say: Look at the end of line one: no semicolon. The compiler reads the whole program before any of it runs, and it refuses this one.
That is a compile-time error: a mistake caught before the program starts. These are the kind ones. You get a line number and a message, and nothing has gone wrong yet.

steps.say: Semicolon fixed, and now every line is legal Java, so the compiler is content. But run it and it crashes on line three: a whole number cannot be divided by zero.

beats.say: Semicolon fixed. Every line is legal Java now, so the compiler is content.
But run it, and it crashes on line three: a whole number cannot be divided by zero.

check.prompt: The compiler accepted it, and then it crashed while running. What kind of error is that?
check.why: Runtime means while the program is running. The code was legal, so the compiler had nothing to object to; the trouble appeared only when that line actually ran.

steps.say: Now it compiles and runs to the end, and prints 48. But I wanted potions per hero, which is 3: I typed * where I meant /. That is a logic error. No message, no crash, just a wrong answer.

beats.say: Now it compiles, runs to the end, and prints 48. But I wanted potions per hero, which is 3. I typed * where I meant /.
That is a logic error: the program does exactly what I wrote, and what I wrote is wrong. No message, no crash. Only checking the output against what you expected will catch it.

outro: “Compile-time, runtime, logic. The last monsters in this hall will make you tell them apart.”

question: A mistake that javac reports before the program is able to start is a {{1}} error. A crash that happens while the program is going is a {{2}} error. A program that finishes normally but gives the wrong answer contains a {{3}} error.
feedback: The three kinds are named for the moment they show up. Compile-time errors are found by the compiler, so the program never starts. Runtime errors get past the compiler because the code is legal, and strike while the program is running. Logic errors never announce themselves at all: the program does exactly what was written, and what was written is wrong.

question:
What kind of error does this line produce?
int price = 4.50;
correct: A compile-time error: a double does not go into an int without help
incorrect: A runtime error: the program starts, then crashes at this line
A logic error: the program runs, but price ends up holding 4
No error: Java drops the .50 and stores 4 in price
feedback: 4.50 is a double, and storing it in an int would lose the .50. Java will not throw information away silently, so the compiler refuses the line ('possible lossy conversion from double to int') and the program never starts. Because it cannot start, it cannot crash or produce a wrong result. The fix is to declare price as a double.

question: Which of these mistakes are reported by the compiler, before the program has run at all?
correct: Leaving the semicolon off the end of a statement
Using Scanner in an ordinary class that has no import line
Spelling a variable's name differently from its declaration
incorrect: Dividing an int by a variable that happens to hold 0
Typing * in a formula where + was what the task needed
The user typing a word when nextInt() expects a number
feedback: The compiler catches whatever breaks the rules of the language: a missing semicolon, a class it has not been told how to find, a name that was never declared (for the last two its message is 'cannot find symbol'). It cannot know what a variable will hold or what a user will type, so dividing by a zero and a word arriving at nextInt() are runtime errors: the program crashes at that line. And the compiler has no idea what you meant, so a legal but wrong formula is a logic error.

The bug is integer division: (a + b) is an int and so is 2, so the half is thrown away. Dividing by 2.0 puts a double on one side, and Java then keeps the fraction. Without the parentheses, a + b / 2.0 divides only b and prints 5.0. Adding 0.0 afterwards is too late, because the half has already gone: that prints 3.0. And % is the remainder, not a division: it prints 1.0.

question: 47 coins are shared among 4 adventurers. What does the last line print?
feedback: Integer division gives each = 11, and the remainder gives left = 3. In the println, the + signs are worked through from left to right. Before any String has appeared, each + left is ordinary addition: 14. Once " and " has been joined on, the left side is a String, so the second each and left are joined on as text, one after the other.
